sentences.text: Romundina was a small, heavily armored acanthothoracid placoderm that lived in shallow marine environments.
The Romundina skull consisted of thin dermal bones heavily ornamented with star-shaped tubercles rich in mesodentine, a tissue type found in teeth.
Romundina is distinguished from previous placoderms by the absence of tesserae between dermal bones on the skull roof, which were fused together.
The star-shaped tubercles on Romundina's skull were likely used for protection against predators.
Romundina had a large protruding bony upper lip that began anterior to the nasal capsule.
Romundina unambiguously possessed a jaw, but its cranial anatomy and brain proportions were more closely aligned with jawless vertebrates.
Research suggests Romundina likely possessed a vascular spine growing just behind the head that served a defensive role.
The primitive tooth-like structures on Romundina's supragnathal plates have a multi-cuspid appearance suggesting tooth-to-tooth occlusion occurred.
Romundina's disorganized dental tubercles resemble the primitive features of Cyclostomes, suggesting organized tooth rows evolved just before the first Gnathostomes.

The first Romundina specimen was discovered in 1975 by Swedish paleontologist Tor Ørvig on Prince of Wales Island in Nunavut, though the genus was originally discovered by the Norwegian paleontologist Tor Ørvig using rocks collected by the geologist Dr. Rómundur Thorsteinsson.

The specimen was found in a 0.5-meter layer taken from the middle of a 12-meter section of unnamed carbonate rocks at locality C-8234, and the original specimen consisted mainly of a head with a complete dermal skull roof and endocranial elements, lacking most of the body.
Tor Ørvig prepared the fossil using a mixture of formic and acetic acid to remove the surrounding rock and reveal a three-dimensional specimen.

Research suggests Romundina primarily ate invertebrates such as crustaceans and worms, utilizing its large crushing tooth-like structures and gnathal plates adapted for eating organisms with hard shells like crustaceans.
The same formation as Romundina contains fossils of arthrodires, heterostracans, gastropods, cephalopods, and corals.
Romundina is characterized as being in the middle of the Placoderm grade.

Romundina lived between 400 and 419 million years ago during the Early Devonian, though other sources state it lived between 419.62 and 393.47 million years ago, spanning from the Lochkovian to the Emsian stages.

Romundina fossils were found near a stream in carbonate rock formations on the western side of Prince of Wales Island in the Canadian Arctic, in an environment likely a shallow water or tidal reef, supported by fossils of corals and other shallow-water organisms found with Romundina.
There is debate over whether the tooth-like structures and gnathal plates of Romundina represent the true primitive condition of Gnathostome dentition.
